Babylon's coming destruction (verses 1–58)

The details of this prophecy are interwoven and repeated.

Babylon possessed enormous treasures, but neither its waters nor its wealth could keep it safe.

Judgment would arrive when the Babylonians least expected it.

Wherever we are—even in the deepest trouble or far from home—we should remember the Lord our God.

At moments of greatest fear or greatest hope, remembering him is especially necessary.

Henry connects the grief caused by Babylon's downfall with the lament over “New Testament Babylon” in Revelation 18:9,19.

He understands the ruin of systems supporting idolatry, unbelief and superstition as clearing the way for a revival of true godliness.

In his prophetic application, a great power characterized by anti-Christian tyranny, idolatry, superstition and persecution of true Christians is as certainly doomed to judgment as ancient Babylon.

This is Henry's interpretation of the later biblical imagery, not a new identification of a particular modern group.

Many people would then mourn their sins and seek the Lord.

The lost sheep of Israel's house would return to the Good Shepherd's fold and no longer wander away.

The exact fulfillment of ancient prophecies strengthens our faith in all God's promises and the prophecies of Scripture.

The written prophecy is sent to Babylon (verses 59–64)

Seraiah was entrusted with taking the prophecy to Babylon and reading it to his fellow Jews in captivity.

Through faith they could look beyond the power oppressing them, foresee its end and be encouraged.

The world offers impressive sights and flattering promises, but Scripture announces that its proud splendor will not last.

The scroll was to be thrown into the Euphrates.

Henry connects that sign to the downfall of New Testament Babylon in Revelation 18:21.

Those who finally sink under God's wrath and curse sink forever.

Babylon and every power that opposes Christ will ultimately fall and not rise again.

Let us hope in God's word and wait quietly for his salvation.

Then we will witness the judgment of wickedness without sharing in its condemnation.

[Jer.51.1-Jer.51.58]
Chapter 51
Babylon's doom; God's controversy with her; encouragements from thence to the Israel of God. ( [Jer.51.1-Jer.51.58] Jr 51:1-58) The confirming of this. ( [Jer.51.59-Jer.51.64] Jr 51:59-64)
Verses 1-58 The particulars of this prophecy are dispersed and interwoven, and the same things left and returned to again. Babylon is abundant in treasures, yet neither her waters nor her wealth shall secure her. Destruction comes when they did not think of it. Wherever we are, in the greatest depths, at the greatest distances, we are to remember the Lord our God; and in the times of the greatest fears and hopes, it is most needful to remember the Lord. The feeling excited by Babylon's fall is the same with the New Testament Babylon, Rev. 18:9,19. The ruin of all who support idolatry, infidelity, and superstition, is needful for the revival of true godliness; and the threatening prophecies of Scripture yield comfort in this view. The great seat of antichristian tyranny, idolatry, and superstition, the persecutor of true Christians, is as certainly doomed to destruction as ancient Babylon. Then will vast multitudes mourn for sin, and seek the Lord. Then will the lost sheep of the house of Israel be brought back to the fold of the good Shepherd, and stray no more. And the exact fulfilment of these ancient prophecies encourages us to faith in all the promises and prophecies of the sacred Scriptures.
[Jer.51.59-Jer.51.64]
Verses 59-64 This prophecy is sent to Babylon, to the captives there, by Seraiah, who is to read it to his countrymen in captivity. Let them with faith see the end of these threatening powers, and comfort themselves herewith. When we see what this world is, how glittering its shows, and how flattering its proposals, let us read in the book of the Lord that it shall shortly be desolate. The book must be thrown into the river Euphrates. The fall of the New Testament Babylon is thus represented, Rev. 18:21. Those that sink under the weight of God's wrath and curse, sink for ever. Babylon, and every antichrist, will soon sink and rise no more for ever. Let us hope in God's word, and quietly wait for his salvation; then we shall see, but shall not share, the destruction of the wicked.

Zedekiah's final defeat (verses 1–11)

Of all the consequences of sin, we should pray most urgently against being cast away from God's presence (Psalm 51:11).

No one is finally removed from his favor without first turning away through sin.

Zedekiah fled, but his escape failed.

There is no escape from divine judgment.

Judgment catches up with the sinner wherever that person runs.

Jerusalem and its temple are destroyed (verses 12–23)

The Chaldean army devastated Jerusalem.

The chapter pays particular attention to the removal of the temple's sacred articles.

Remembering their beauty and value helps us understand how serious the people's sin was, since that sin brought about such devastation.

Judah's leaders are carried away (verses 24–30)

The leaders of the Jews had led the people astray.

Now those leaders themselves became especially visible examples of the Lord's righteous judgment.

The narrative also records two earlier deportations.

This people repeatedly became a remarkable example of both divine judgment and divine mercy.

Jehoiachin is raised from prison (verses 31–34)

For the fuller historical account of Jehoiachin's release and promotion, see 2 Kings 25:27–30.

Those living under oppression may take encouragement that waiting quietly for the Lord's salvation is not in vain.

Our times are in God's hand.

So are the hearts of everyone with whom we have dealings.

May we grow increasingly able to rest upon the Rock of Ages.

May we look forward in holy faith to the hour when God restores Zion and overthrows every enemy of his church.

Verses 1-11 This fruit of sin we should pray against above any thing; Cast me not away from thy presence, Ps. 51:11. None are cast out of God's presence but those who by sin have first thrown themselves out. Zedekiah's flight was in vain, for there is no escaping the judgments of God; they come upon the sinner, and overtake him, let him flee where he will.
[Jer.52.12-Jer.52.23]
Verses 12-23 The Chaldean army made woful havoc. But nothing is so particularly related here, as the carrying away of the articles in the temple. The remembrance of their beauty and value shows us the more the evil of sin.
[Jer.52.24-Jer.52.30]
Verses 24-30 The leaders of the Jews caused them to err; but now they are, in particular, made monuments of Divine justice. Here is an account of two earlier captivities. This people often were wonders both of judgment and mercy.
[Jer.52.31-Jer.52.34]
Verses 31-34 See this history of king Jehoiachin in II Kin. 25:27-30. Those under oppression will find it is not in vain for them to hope and quietly to wait for the salvation of the Lord. Our times are in God's hand, for the hearts of all we have to deal with are so. May we be enabled, more and more, to rest on the Rock of Ages, and to look forward with holy faith to that hour, when the Lord will bring again Zion, and overthrow all the enemies of the church.
